entries.purpose: Protect a stored member or administrator password against an attacker who reads the database
entries.storageBoundary: The instance database, in user_account.password_hash. The salt and the parameters travel inside the encoding; there is no separate key.
entries.permittedUse: Verifying a sign-in and re-encoding a stored hash that sits below the current parameters. Never for a digest, an identifier or a signature.
entries.rotation: Raising the memory cost or the iteration count is the rotation, and a stored hash below either is re-encoded on its owner's next successful sign-in; storing that is best effort, so a database failure leaves the old hash in place rather than failing the login. Spring Security compares only those two, so changing the parallelism, the salt length or the hash length alone does not re-encode anything already stored, and existing hashes keep the parameters they were written with until one of the other two moves.
entries.revocation: Issuing a new credential replaces the hash and ends every session of the account.
entries.recovery: None is possible or needed: a hash is not recoverable by design, and a member who cannot sign in is given a new credential.
entries.retirement: Argon2id is replaced by encoding new and re-encoded passwords under the successor while the old encoding stays verifiable, which is what the re-encode path already does for a parameter change.

entries.purpose: The one-time password an instance mails a member for their first sign-in
entries.storageBoundary: Generated in memory, mailed to the member, and kept only as its Argon2id hash. The plaintext is never written to the database, a log or an administrative screen.
entries.permittedUse: One sign-in, after which the account must set a permanent password. It cannot become that permanent password.
entries.rotation: Issuing a credential again replaces the previous one and ends every session of the account.
entries.revocation: Withdrawing an unused credential clears the hash and its deadline.
entries.recovery: None: a lost credential is reissued, never recovered.
entries.retirement: Retired with the account, whose deactivation ends its sessions.

entries.purpose: Give an account with no credential a hash that no input can match, so an absent password is not an empty one
entries.storageBoundary: In memory only. The component is a singleton, so one value exists per process and it is discarded after encoding; nothing ever needs to reproduce it.
entries.permittedUse: Standing in for a credential that does not exist. It is never sent, shown, or successfully verified against a member's input.
entries.rotation: Every process start generates a new one. Nothing depends on the value, so there is no schedule to keep.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is possible, which is the point.
entries.retirement: Replaced with the password-hashing entry it shares an algorithm with.

entries.purpose: Give a stored row an identifier that names it without describing anybody
entries.storageBoundary: The instance database, as the primary key of the row it names, and the public API, which addresses rows by it.
entries.permittedUse: Naming a row. An identifier authenticates nothing and is not a capability: every endpoint that takes one still authorises the caller.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: an identifier that changed would no longer name the same row.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed.
entries.retirement: Not applicable while the schema addresses rows this way.

entries.purpose: Name a signed-in member's session, which is what the session cookie carries
entries.storageBoundary: Spring Session generates the value and stores the session in the instance database; the identifier travels in the host-bound session cookie. This project neither generates nor formats it, which is why no parameters are recorded here.
entries.permittedUse: Identifying a session. It is a bearer credential: whoever holds it is signed in, which is why the cookie is HttpOnly, Secure and host-bound and why every credential change ends the sessions of that account.
entries.rotation: A new session is issued on sign-in, and the previous session of that account is ended. There is no separate rotation schedule.
entries.revocation: Signing out, a credential change, a deactivation and the session-limit displacement each end sessions server-side, so a revoked identifier stops working rather than merely expiring.
entries.recovery: None is needed: an ended session is replaced by signing in again.
entries.retirement: Follows Spring Session; a successor scheme takes effect for sessions created after it.

entries.purpose: Prove that a state-changing request came from this application's own pages
entries.storageBoundary: Spring Security generates the value and places it in a cookie the frontend reads and echoes in a header. Nothing is stored server-side and this project does not generate the value.
entries.permittedUse: Comparing a request's header against its cookie. It is not an authenticator: it says the request came from this origin, never who made it.
entries.rotation: A new token is issued with the session it belongs to.
entries.revocation: Ending the session ends the token with it.
entries.recovery: None is needed.
entries.retirement: Follows Spring Security.

entries.purpose: Count failed sign-ins per client address, and instance-wide, without keeping the address in the counter
entries.storageBoundary: The instance database, as login_attempt_limit.subject_hash, where it is part of the primary key. It is written on every counted attempt and removed by the retention sweep that clears expired windows.
entries.permittedUse: Grouping attempts by address and instance-wide. The digest is not an authenticator, and it is not a pseudonym that may be published: the space of client addresses is small enough to search exhaustively, so a stored digest is a stored address with an extra step.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: no key exists. Rows age out with their window rather than being rotated.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed; the counters rebuild themselves from subsequent attempts.
entries.retirement: A successor digest changes what the stored subjects mean, so the existing rows are cleared with the change rather than migrated. Nothing outside the limiter reads them.

entries.purpose: Recognise a repeated booking request so a retry does not create a second booking
entries.storageBoundary: The instance database, beside the booking it identifies.
entries.permittedUse: Comparing one request to another, and only within the bookings of the member who sent it. It carries no security claim and protects nothing.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: no key.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed; it is recomputed from what it names.
entries.retirement: Replaceable with any digest, since nothing outside the instance reads it.

entries.purpose: Name the stored club logo so a browser can be told whether its copy is current
entries.storageBoundary: The instance database, and the ETag it becomes.
entries.permittedUse: Cache validation. It is not an integrity guarantee against a party that can write the row.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: no key.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed; it is recomputed from what it names.
entries.retirement: Replaceable with any digest; a changed algorithm invalidates caches once.

entries.purpose: Match an imported row against a person already on the roster
entries.storageBoundary: The instance database, on the imported reference.
entries.permittedUse: Deduplicating an import. It is not a pseudonym that may be published: it is taken over a name, an address and a membership type, whose space is small enough to search.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: no key.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed; it is recomputed from what it names.
entries.retirement: A change re-matches every stored reference, so it is made with an import run rather than in place.

entries.purpose: Name the seeded assessment dataset so a report says which data it was produced against
entries.storageBoundary: Computed at runtime from a constant in the image; nothing is stored.
entries.permittedUse: Identifying a dataset in a report.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: no key.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed; it is recomputed from what it names.
entries.retirement: Replaceable with any digest.

entries.purpose: Give a submitted booking a client-side identity so a retry is recognised
entries.storageBoundary: The browser, for the life of one submission.
entries.permittedUse: Identifying a request. It authenticates nothing, which is why the non-secure-context fallback is acceptable.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: every submission generates one.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed.
entries.retirement: Replaceable without a migration.

entries.purpose: Name an artefact, a configuration or a report the verification harness produced, so two runs can be compared
entries.storageBoundary: Build output and workflow artefacts. Nothing reaches an instance.
entries.permittedUse: Comparing and naming artefacts. No harness digest is a security control, and none may be presented as evidence that content was not tampered with by a party who could write it.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: no key.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed; a rerun recomputes everything.
entries.retirement: Replaceable with any digest.

entries.purpose: Give a verification run values nothing else uses, such as a scratch database name, a throwaway password or a correlation id
entries.storageBoundary: The lifetime of one verification run. Nothing is written to a tracked file and nothing reaches an instance.
entries.permittedUse: Test fixtures and correlation only. No harness value ever becomes an operational credential.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: every run generates its own.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed.
entries.retirement: Replaceable without a migration.

entries.purpose: Generate the throwaway certificates and key pairs a verification run needs to exercise a TLS path
entries.storageBoundary: A temporary directory for the life of one run, and never a tracked file. Every certificate is self-signed, valid for a day, and issued to a name under a reserved example domain.
entries.permittedUse: Standing up a relay or a proxy a test then connects to. No generated key is ever trusted by an instance, published, or reused across runs.
entries.rotation: Each run generates its own; there is nothing that outlives a run to rotate.
entries.revocation: Not applicable: no party trusts these beyond the run that made them.
entries.recovery: None is needed; a rerun generates new material.
entries.retirement: Replaced by whatever the tested transport requires.

entries.purpose: Recognise one expected certificate by its digest instead of trusting whoever a certificate authority vouched for
entries.storageBoundary: The expected value is held outside the code that checks it: a repository variable for the evidence recipient, a launch argument for a browser, an environment value for the mail peer. No digest of a production certificate is tracked in this repository.
entries.permittedUse: Deciding whether the party at the other end is the expected one. Unlike the content hashes above, this is a security control: a mismatch refuses the connection or blocks the seal rather than being reported.
entries.rotation: Replacing the pinned certificate means replacing the expectation in the same change; the two are held apart on purpose, so changing only one fails closed.
entries.revocation: Removing the expectation stops the pinned path rather than falling back to an unpinned one.
entries.recovery: A pin that no longer matches is a refusal, not a loss: the expectation is corrected and the run repeated.
entries.retirement: A successor digest is introduced by pinning under it before the previous expectation is removed.

entries.purpose: Let anybody verify that a published image was built by this repository's release workflow
entries.storageBoundary: No long-lived private key exists. Sigstore issues a short-lived certificate against the workflow's OIDC identity and records the signature in a public transparency log.
entries.permittedUse: Signing a published image. It says which workflow built the image, not that the image is free of defects.
entries.rotation: Every signing operation obtains a new short-lived certificate; there is nothing to rotate on a schedule.
entries.revocation: Not applicable to a keyless signature. A withdrawn release is deleted and stated as withdrawn.
entries.recovery: None is possible or needed: no material can be lost, and a signature is produced again by re-running the release.
entries.retirement: Replaced by changing the signing action, which changes what a verifier is told to expect.

entries.purpose: Publish where an image came from and what it contains, signed by the workflow that built it
entries.storageBoundary: Same keyless identity as the release signature; the attestation is pushed to the registry beside the image.
entries.permittedUse: Attesting build provenance and the software bill of materials. It records what a build did, not that the result is correct.
entries.rotation: Each run attests under its own short-lived certificate.
entries.revocation: Not applicable to a keyless attestation.
entries.recovery: None is possible or needed.
entries.retirement: Replaced by changing the attesting action.

entries.purpose: Encrypt the protected part of a security assessment so only its custodian can read it
entries.storageBoundary: The recipient certificate is tracked; the value it is checked against lives in a GitHub repository variable outside commit history, and the private key never enters this repository. The operational record is .github/security-evidence-key.json, which holds the custodian role and the decrypt-canary window and deliberately no second copy of that value.
entries.permittedUse: Sealing assessment evidence for its custodian. It is not a general-purpose encryption facility and no instance data passes through it.
entries.rotation: Replacing the recipient certificate means replacing the tracked certificate and the repository variable, which are separately held on purpose: changing only one blocks sealing rather than sealing to the wrong recipient.
entries.revocation: Removing the repository variable blocks sealing at the next run.
entries.recovery: A lost private key makes existing envelopes unreadable and cannot be recovered. That is bounded by the decrypt canary, which proves the key is still usable within its recorded window; a canary that cannot be verified is the signal to reseal under a new recipient.
entries.retirement: A successor recipient is introduced by sealing to it and letting the canary window of the previous one lapse.

entries.purpose: Encrypt and authenticate what a member's browser sends to the instance
entries.storageBoundary: The reverse proxy's own storage. For a club's own domain the proxy obtains the certificate itself and Courtside never sees the key. The verification profiles are different and say so: they run the proxy with an internal certificate authority, so a local root and its leaf keys exist inside those containers for the life of a run.
entries.permittedUse: The public entry point. Courtside ships no production certificate authority, generates no production key material and states no cipher list of its own. The internal authority is for the verification profiles and must not be used to serve a club.
entries.rotation: The proxy obtains and renews certificates itself; an operator supplying their own owns the renewal.
entries.revocation: The issuing authority's, and the operator's to request.
entries.recovery: A lost certificate is reissued by the authority; nothing in Courtside needs to be recovered with it.
entries.retirement: Follows what the proxy supports.

entries.purpose: Encrypt and authenticate the connection an instance hands its outgoing messages to
entries.storageBoundary: The relay's certificate, read by the instance. In the reference deployment the proxy's certificate pair for the mail hostname is copied into a volume the mail container reads, so that deployment does hold a private key on the operator's own host; nothing is copied out of it and no key is tracked in this repository.
entries.permittedUse: Reaching the relay over an encrypted connection. STARTTLS is required rather than opportunistic, so a relay that cannot negotiate it is refused instead of being spoken to in the clear. Trusting an unverified relay certificate is a deliberate, separately named setting.
entries.rotation: The relay's own renewal, which the instance observes rather than performs; a certificate whose remaining life falls below the configured share is reported.
entries.revocation: The issuing authority's.
entries.recovery: A relay that cannot present a usable certificate refuses the connection, and the message is retried four times over about a minute. After that the message is recorded as failed, and failed is terminal: nothing redelivers it later, so a relay outage longer than that ladder loses the send and the message log is where an operator sees it.
entries.retirement: Follows the relay.

entries.purpose: Sign outgoing mail so a receiving server can tell it came from the club's domain
entries.storageBoundary: The mail container's volume in the reference deployment, where the container generates the key itself. The public half is a DNS record the operator publishes. No key is tracked in this repository.
entries.permittedUse: Signing the club's own outgoing mail.
entries.rotation: The operator publishes a new selector, signs under it, and retires the old record once nothing in flight relies on it.
entries.revocation: Removing the DNS record for a selector.
entries.recovery: A lost key is replaced by generating a new one under a new selector; no past message needs to be recoverable.
entries.retirement: The selector's DNS record is withdrawn after the change has propagated.

entries.purpose: Carry the instance's database traffic, which includes session rows, password hashes and the hashed login subjects
entries.algorithm: TLS, when an operator requires it; the driver's own opportunistic default otherwise
entries.storageBoundary: The connection between the application container and the database container, and the operator's own authority file where one is configured. Courtside reads that file and holds no material of its own; the reference deployment ships no certificate and defaults to the driver's opportunistic mode, which encrypts when the database offers it and verifies nothing.
entries.permittedUse: Reaching the database. `courtside.database.tls.mode` decides what that means: `prefer` leaves the driver alone, `disable` refuses encryption, and `verify-full` requires a certificate that chains to the configured authority and names the host the connection URL names. Verified mode refuses to start when the authority is missing or unreadable, and when the connection URL carries an argument that would override it.
entries.rotation: The operator's, on their own authority and server certificate. Courtside reads the authority file for every new connection, so a replaced file takes effect without a restart and a replaced one that no longer vouches for the database refuses the next connection rather than falling back.
entries.revocation: The issuing authority's. Courtside performs no revocation check of its own.
entries.recovery: An authority file that no longer matches is a refusal, not a loss: the operator restores the right file, or sets the mode back to `prefer`.
entries.retirement: Encrypting the reverse proxy's connection to the application is the remaining half of this path and is tracked as its own work.
